The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. case_info.explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.

case_info.caption: Admission electrocardiogram (ECG) showing type A preexcitation syndrome, with an upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and positive T waves in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave. These changes were suggestive of a de Winter ECG pattern.
case_info.explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.

case_info.caption: Admission electrocardiogram (ECG) showing type A preexcitation syndrome, with an upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and positive T waves in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave. These changes were suggestive of a de Winter ECG pattern.
case_info.explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.

case_info.explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.
